title: History of Pakistan
wiki_lead:
The history of Pakistan preceding the country's independence in 1947 is shared with that of neighbouring Afghanistan, India, Iran and Tibet. Spanning the western expanse of the Indian subcontinent and the eastern borderlands of the Iranian plateau, the region of contemporary Pakistan served both as the fertile ground of a major civilization and as the gateway of South Asia to Central Asia and the Near East.
Situated on the first coastal migration route of Homo sapiens out of Africa, the region was inhabited early by modern humans. The 9,000-year history of village life in South Asia traces back to the Neolithic (7000–4300 BCE) site of Mehrgarh in Pakistan,  and the 5,000-year history of urban life in South Asia to the various sites of the Indus Valley Civilisation, including Mohenjo-daro and Harappa.
The ensuing millennia saw the region of present-day Pakistan absorb diverse influences. Several ancient empires left their mark in the region, such as the Achaemenid, the Maurya, the Indo-Greek, the Indo-Scythian, the Indo-Parthian, the Kushan, the Apracha and the Odi in Gandhara, the Huna and the Takka; as did, after the Islamic conquest, the Umayyad, the Ghaznavid, the Ghurid, the Delhi Sultanate, and the Mughal, before the modern period. During the medieval period, dynasties originating from the modern-day country ruled various areas in and around Pakistan, including the Patola, the Odi, the Soomra, the Samma, the Qambrani, the Langah, the Sayyid and the Lodi of Delhi Sultanate, the Gibari, the Shah Miri, the Maqpon, the Kalhora, the Talpur, the Gichki, the Sukerchakia, and the Daudpotra, among others.
Gradually, in the first half of the 19th century, the region came under suzerainty of the East India Company through conquests and subsidiary alliances. Company Raj was replaced by the direct crown rule, the British Raj, after 1858. In the early decades of the 20th-century, Muslim nationalism gained momentum in the predominantly Muslim population and intelligentsia, and the Pakistan Movement, led by Muhammad Ali Jinnah, ended with the partition of British holdings in 1947 and the establishment of the dominions of Pakistan and India. The heritage of the country is represented among others in the ancient, mainly Hindu-Buddhist, sites of Taxila, and Takht-i-Bahi, the 14th-century Islamic-Sindhi monuments of Thatta, and the 17th-century Mughal monuments of Lahore.

Prehistory


Paleolithic period
The Soanian is an archaeological culture of the Lower Paleolithic, Acheulean. It is named after the Soan Valley in the Sivalik Hills, near modern-day Islamabad and is dated between c.774,000 and c.11,700 BCE.


Neolithic period

Mehrgarh is an important Neolithic site discovered in 1974, which shows early evidence of farming and herding, and dentistry. The site dates back to 7000–5500 BCE and is located on the Kachi Plain of Balochistan. The residents of Mehrgarh lived in mud brick houses, stored grain in granaries, fashioned tools from copper, cultivated barley, wheat, jujubes and dates, and herded sheep, goats and cattle. As the civilisation progressed (5500–2600 BCE) residents began to engage in crafts, including flint knapping, tanning, bead production, and metalworking. The site was occupied continuously until 2600 BCE, when climatic changes began to occur. Between 2600 and 2000 BCE, region became more arid and Mehrgarh was abandoned in favour of the Indus Valley, where a new civilisation was in the early stages of development.


Bronze Age


Indus Valley Civilisation

The Bronze Age in the Indus Valley began around 3300 BCE with the Indus Valley Civilization. Along with ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia, it was one of three early civilisations of the Old World, and of the three the most widespread, covering an area of 1.25 million km2. grok_lead: The history of Pakistan documents a region within the Indian subcontinent that encompasses the succession of civilizations, empires, and political entities within the modern territory of Pakistan, commencing with the Bronze Age Indian subcontinental urban society, the Indus Valley Civilization, from approximately 3300 to 1300 BCE, an early Bronze Age urban society characterized by planned cities, advanced sanitation, and trade networks extending to Mesopotamia, with major sites including Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, discovered during the British India period, located in present-day Sindh and Punjab provinces; later, the northwestern Indian subcontinental region encompassed a significant portion of ancient Indo-Aryan Vedic Hindu heritage. This era was followed by invasions and rule under the Achaemenid Empire, Alexander the Great in 326 BCE, the Mauryan Empire under Ashoka, Greco-Buddhist kingdom of the Indo-Greeks and the syncretic Kushan Empire, and Hindu dynasties such as the Gupta influence, followed by local Buddhist and Hindu polities such as the Rai dynasty (Buddhist) and Chach dynasty (Hindu Brahmin), before the arrival of Islam via Arab conquests in the 8th century CE. A defining shift occurred with the Umayyad Caliphate's conquest in 711â712 CE, led by Muhammad bin Qasim, who defeated Hindu ruler Raja Dahir and established the first enduring Muslim governance in the Indian subcontinent. Afterwards, medieval Sindh witnessed indigenous dynasties such as the Soomra (1024â1351 CE, possibly from the Parmar Rajput tribe) and Samma (1351â1524 CE, possibly of Rajput tribal origin), and the Punjab region was governed by the Hindu Shahis, leading to the establishment of Muslim sultanates including the Ghaznavids and Ghurids by the 11th-12th centuries. Subsequent centuries saw the Delhi Sultanate 's extension into the region, peaking under the Mughal Empire from the 16th to 19th centuries, which centralized administration, promoted Turkic-led Persianate culture, and built architectural landmarks like the Lahore Fort, though marked by regional autonomy and eventual decline. This decline accelerated amid the northward expansion of the Hindu Maratha Empire under leaders like Mahadji Scindia into Punjab and the Doab regions following recovery from the 1761 Third Battle of Panipat, and the rise of Sikh Mislsâconfederacies of warrior groups that unified territories through guerrilla warfare and political alliances, laying the foundation for Maharaja Ranjit Singh 's Sikh Empire, which encompassed Punjab including large parts of present-day Pakistan and effectively supplanted Mughal authority. British colonial rule consolidated after the 1849 annexation of Punjab and the 1857 suppression of the Indian Rebellion, integrating the area into the British Raj until the 1947 partition of India, driven by the Muslim League's demand for a separate homeland for Indian Muslims under Muhammad Ali Jinnah. Pakistan's founding is associated with the vision of Muhammad Iqbal and the leadership of Muhammad Ali Jinnah, and the Two-Nation theory, an idea championed by the All-India Muslim League and many Indian Muslims, which asserts that Muslims and Hindus in British India formed two distinct nationsâexemplified by the All-India Muslim League's call for Direct Action Day on 16 August 1946, when Muslim Leagueâs Muhammad Ali Jinnah declared the only possibilities were "either a divided India or a destroyed India"âwhich led to communal riots, particularly the Great Calcutta Killings in Calcutta and the Noakhali riots and Tippera violence (present-day Comilla), involving attacks by Muslim League-aligned mobs on Hindus and Sikhs resulting in thousands of deaths, displacements, and atrocities including abductions and assaults on non-Muslim women and childrenâ, resulting in Pakistan's independence on August 14, 1947, but accompanied by partition riots that caused 12-15 million displacements and hundreds of thousands to over a million deaths from communal violence, particularly targeting Hindus and Sikhs in territories that became Pakistan and, later, Bangladesh, and reducing the indigenous Hindu and Sikh populations to marginal minorities. Since independence, Pakistan has navigated foundational challenges including the 1947-1948 Indo-Pakistani War over Kashmir, the 1956 republican constitution, military coups in 1958 by Ayub Khan and 1977 by Zia-ul-Haq imposing Islamization policies, the 1971 war leading to East Pakistan's secession as Bangladesh, economic nationalization under Zulfikar Ali Bhutto followed by his 1979 execution, democratic transitions marred by corruption allegations, the 1998 nuclear tests amid sanctions, and post-2001 counterterrorism efforts against Taliban-linked militancy, alongside persistent issues of governance instability, ethnic tensions, and economic volatility despite growth in agriculture and remittances.
